issues.legal_issue: Subletting may be established by inferring monetary consideration from exclusive possession and the tenant’s failure to provide an acceptable explanation, without direct proof of payment.
material_facts: The lease document stated that the tenant took the premises for his own business and undertook not to part with possession or permit another person to occupy them.
The tenant’s son was found in exclusive possession, conducting an independent business and living separately from the tenant.
The tenant’s explanation that he had taken the premises for his son was rejected.
There was no direct evidence of payment or a promise of payment by the son to the tenant.
issues.conclusion: The finding of subletting was lawful because the tenant had parted with possession and the son’s exclusive possession, together with the rejected explanation, permitted an inference of monetary consideration despite the absence of direct proof of payment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 13 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Control Act, the landlord bears the burden of proving subletting. Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. S.B. Sardar Ranjit Singh and Shama Prashant Raje v. Ganpatrao state that parting with possession and monetary consideration are the two ingredients. Bharat Sales Ltd. v. Life Insurance Corporation of India explains that the clandestine nature of subletting can make direct proof of an agreement or payment difficult, and that payment may be inferred from proved facts, including exclusive possession. Smt. Rajbir Kaur v. M/s S. Chokesiri and Co. permits an inference of monetary consideration from exclusive possession and an unacceptable explanation, while Kala v. Madho Parshad Vaidya states that, once parting with possession is established, the evidential onus shifts to the tenant to explain the possession. Direct proof of monetary consideration is not a sine qua non.

rule.if: eviction_case_based_on_subletting and tenant_parted_possession and occupant_exclusive_possession and tenant_explanation_rejected

predicates.eviction_case_based_on_subletting: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.tenant_parted_possession: The tenant gave up possession of the premises, wholly or in part, to another person.
predicates.occupant_exclusive_possession: Another person was found in exclusive possession of the premises or the relevant part.
predicates.tenant_explanation_rejected: The tenant’s explanation for the other person’s possession was not accepted.

issues.definition: When eviction is sought for subletting and the tenant has parted with possession to an occupant in exclusive possession whose possession the tenant cannot satisfactorily explain, subletting may be inferred without direct proof of payment.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant’s relationship with the person in exclusive possession does not by itself prevent a finding of subletting.
material_facts: The occupant was the tenant’s son, but they lived separately.
The son was found in exclusive possession of the premises and conducted an independent business there.
The son had no contractual relationship with the landlady, who had let the premises to the tenant.
The tenant had undertaken not to part with possession or allow another person to occupy the premises.
issues.conclusion: The fact that the occupant was the tenant’s son did not prevent a finding of subletting; the relationship between tenant and occupant was not material to that determination.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Control Act prohibits subletting without the landlord’s written consent. The relevant question is whether the tenant parted with possession to another person, not whether that person is related to the tenant. Bhairab Chandra Nandan v. Ranadhir Chandra Dutta rejected the view that a family relationship alone makes the occupant a licensee rather than a subtenant.

predicates.eviction_case_based_on_subletting: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant had sublet the premises.
predicates.occupant_exclusive_possession: Another person was found in exclusive possession of the premises or the relevant part.
predicates.occupant_related_to_tenant: The person in exclusive possession was related to the tenant.
predicates.occupant_has_no_contractual_relationship: The person in exclusive possession had no contractual relationship with the landlord concerning the premises.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding based on subletting, an occupant’s relationship to the tenant does not prevent a finding of subletting when the occupant has exclusive possession and no contractual relationship with the landlord.

issues.legal_issue: An unpleaded and unproved claim of waiver cannot defeat eviction for subletting without the landlord’s written consent.
material_facts: The tenant and occupant argued that the landlady knew the occupant was conducting business in the premises and continued to receive rent.
Waiver had not been pleaded before the Rent Controller, the Appellate Authority, or the High Court; it was raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The tenant did not claim to have obtained the landlady’s written consent to sublet the premises.
issues.conclusion: The waiver argument could not be raised for the first time in the Supreme Court and, in any event, could not defeat the statutory requirement of written consent on the basis of a bald, unproved plea.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2)(ii)(a) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Control Act requires the landlord’s written consent for subletting. Waiver is a question of fact that must be expressly pleaded and clearly proved, and a bald plea cannot defeat the statutory requirement. The Court relied on M/s Shalimar Tar Products Ltd. v. H.C. Sharma and Pulin Behari Lal v. Mahadeb Dutta.

predicates.eviction_case_based_on_unconsented_suble: A landlord sought eviction on the ground that the tenant sublet the premises without the landlord’s written consent.
predicates.waiver_not_pleaded_below: The tenant did not plead waiver before the lower decision-making bodies and raised it only at a later appellate stage.
predicates.written_consent_absent: The tenant did not obtain or claim to have obtained the landlord’s written consent to sublet.

issues.definition: When eviction is sought for subletting without written consent, a waiver claim not pleaded below cannot defeat eviction.
